summary: A white marble memorial light on Belle Isle in the Detroit River, lit in 1930 for William Livingstone of the Lake Carriers' Association; the island's earlier light stood nearby.

lens.note: Fourth-order lens fitted with an electric lamp (Bulletin, 1930); its origin is disputed (see notes_for_editor)

structures.type: fluted octagonal shaft on an octagonal platform
structures.note: Shaft 47 ft high per the 1930 Bulletin; the Detroit Historical Society gives 58 ft for the whole structure

access.note: Grounds open, tower closed to visitors (LighthouseFriends). The USLHS place record says Open to Public: No.

visit.note: The Dossin Great Lakes Museum, elsewhere on Belle Isle, has a collection of Fresnel lenses

events.note: Livingstone Channel opened to commerce on 19 October 1912; the Service lit its marks as the channel was finished
Lighthouse Service reports the light in commission in June 1930; LighthouseFriends gives 8 April 1930 as the start of operation
Designed by Albert Kahn; ornament by Geza Maroti; built of Georgia marble at a cost of $100,000
Dedicated 17 October 1930, the fifth anniversary of Livingstone's death; H. D. King, Deputy Commissioner of Lighthouses, gave the address
Thieves broke in and took two of the four lights from the lantern room; the city later fenced the tower
Second break-in; graffiti sprayed on a temporary plastic lens

notes_for_editor: (1) Start of operation: LighthouseFriends says 8 April 1930; Wikipedia (not cited) says 6 April. The 1 June 1930 Bulletin says only that the light is now in commission. (2) Designer: LighthouseFriends and the Detroit Historical Society credit Albert Kahn with the design, Maroti with the ornament. Wikipedia says Maroti designed it and Kahn supervised, attributing that to the Detroit Free Press through a citation we did not read; not used. (3) Height: the 1930 Bulletin gives the shaft as 47 ft (14 m, the structures height_m above); DHS gives 58 ft for the whole structure. The story states both. (4) Lens origin: DHS says the lens came from the old Belle Isle light; LighthouseFriends says a lens now at Beaver Island was reportedly used at the memorial for fifty years. Unresolved. (5) Present signal: LighthouseFriends says alternating white and red flashes every ten seconds; the record says Oc W 4s (Wikipedia cites the Light List). We could not open the Light List (navcen.uscg.gov returned HTTP 403), so the characteristic is unverified. (6) Public access: LighthouseFriends says grounds open, tower closed; the USLHS place record says Open to Public: No. (7) LighthouseFriends says the 1980 thieves took two of four 'lenses'; DHS says two of four 'lamps'. The story says 'lights'. (8) The old Belle Isle light's position: LighthouseFriends says the southeast point; Wikipedia says The Strand (not cited). The us-mi-belle-isle record is lost. (9) The Bulletin's OCR is interleaved across columns on PDF p. 21; the quotes used are single column runs and were checked against the cached text. Bulletin 1930 p. 21 printed pagination not read; PDF pages used. (10) No storm, wreck or rescue is recorded for this light in the sources read. (11) The Commissioner's 1915 report: printed p. 57, scan p. 62 (the OCR page header is read as 57). (12) Not read: Detroit Free Press, Historic Detroit, the Light List, Dime Savings or Lake Carriers' archives. (13) The 1990s restoration and the 1954-1969 Army occupation appear only in Wikipedia and are left out. (14) Candlepower: the 1930 Bulletin gives about 11,500 candlepower; DHS gives an 8600-candlepower beacon. The story states both. (15) Keepers: the roster (USLHS place belle-isle, showPeople/8500) and LighthouseFriends name keepers of the OLDER Belle Isle light, not of the memorial; the memorial names none, so keepers is empty for this record. (16) H. D. King: the 1930 Bulletin (PDF p. 42) and its index give 'H. D. King'; LighthouseFriends prints 'H.S. King'. The story follows the Bulletin. (17) Beaver Island lens: LighthouseFriends' note quotes an informational sign at Beaver Island Lighthouse; the story attributes the 'reportedly used for fifty years' statement to that sign, via LighthouseFriends. (18) Wayne County is not in the sources read; the story now says Detroit, Michigan, which LighthouseFriends and DHS support. (19) Verification pass 2026-10-28: the story was reworded where it followed the Bulletin's sentences closely, the keepers section moved under its own heading, and the 'beside the island' location for Livingstone Channel was removed (LighthouseFriends places it in the lower Detroit River only).
